# Testing Strategy

## Purpose

RelayView uses a layered testing strategy shaped like a testing pyramid. Most
behavior should be verified by deterministic unit and bounded-integration tests.
Progressively smaller suites exercise the built browser, the assembled production
workflow, and finally real model-provider behavior.

This document defines the responsibility of each layer and the defaults for
placing new coverage. It intentionally does not prescribe fixed test counts or
ratios. The important invariant is that most behavioral coverage remains below
the browser and real-provider layers, while a small number of higher-level tests
prove that the boundaries compose correctly.

Tests are specification artifacts. A behavioral change is incomplete until the
appropriate layer verifies its success path, important failures, recovery or
state transitions, and externally visible contract.

## Layers

| Layer | Primary commands | Responsibility | Default characteristics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit and bounded integration | `npm test` | Domain logic, state machines, storage, API and protocol contracts, security boundaries, adapters, and focused process interactions | Numerous, deterministic, isolated, and as fast as the boundary permits |
| Browser integration | `npm run test:browser` | Built Lit UI behavior, routing, component contracts, owner-client integration, accessibility-relevant controls, responsive layout, and large-data behavior | Fewer scenarios using controlled fixtures; assertions focus on behavior and rendered state |
| Seeded production showcase | `npm run test:showcase` | Production browser, owner API, durable store, event path, supervisor, and Git-status presentation with representative pre-populated state | Small deterministic suite for assembled evidence surfaces and stable visual review |
| Empty-state production workflow | `npm run test:workflow` | Public New Task submission through planner finalization, automatic implementation handoff, validation, Git isolation, session control, restart/recovery, and typed failure behavior | Very small deterministic end-to-end suite using Pi-compatible fake processes and real local infrastructure boundaries |
| Real-profile smoke | Manifest-backed workflow smoke and documented admission checks | Actual Pi and model-provider usability, credential delivery, model assignment, tool loops, and a real repository edit | Narrow, explicit, potentially costly, and run only when the affected provider or production boundary requires it |

The first layer is not required to consist only of pure in-memory unit tests.
SQLite, filesystem, subprocess, and assembled-service tests belong there when
those dependencies are the smallest useful boundary for the behavior. Keep each
test focused and deterministic, and avoid promoting coverage to Playwright merely
because the implementation crosses modules.

## Choosing A Layer

Place a regression at the lowest layer that can faithfully prove the behavior:

1. Prefer a focused Vitest test for logic, persistence, protocol, state, failure,
   recovery, and security invariants.
2. Add browser integration coverage when correctness depends on rendering,
   browser events, focus, responsive layout, accessibility semantics, routing,
   or the browser-facing client contract.
3. Extend a production-path workflow scenario only when the risk is in the
   composition of owner, store, events, process supervision, Git, private tools,
   and browser behavior. Prefer extending an existing scenario over adding a new
   full lifecycle when that preserves fault isolation and readability.
4. Require a real-profile smoke only when deterministic substitutes cannot prove
   provider compatibility, credentials, model assignment, or actual model/tool
   behavior.

Higher-level coverage complements rather than replaces lower-level coverage. A
workflow regression should normally have focused tests for its important domain
and failure rules, while the workflow test proves that those rules remain wired
together through production boundaries.

## Determinism And Isolation

The default automated suites must not depend on public network access, provider
availability, production credentials, or nondeterministic model output. Use
controlled clocks, fixtures, disposable repositories and databases, and
Pi-compatible fake processes as appropriate. Tests must not read or retain
credentials, private provider diagnostics, or unrelated host state.

Process-backed tests remain part of the normal Vitest layer but must have bounded
startup, shutdown, output, and failure behavior. The standard `npm test` command
caps Vitest at four workers because greater file concurrency reproducibly caused
unrelated process-backed failures; see
[Source Layout And Retrieval Evidence](../historical/issue-259-source-layout-evidence.md).

Test files importing `src/api/api-test-fixtures.ts` use a 30-second default
through Vitest's file-local runtime configuration. These bounded integration
suites include Git, SQLite, HTTP schema setup, workflow execution, and shutdown.
<!-- keep-issue-ref: verification-run — the 30-second budget's only support is these two identified measurement runs -->
Two measurements support that budget. During #402 acceptance, seven cases across
benchmark, workflow, HTTP client, and task-memory suites exceeded the generic
five-second default; all completed their assertions in roughly 4.7–6.3 seconds in
isolated diagnostics. During #516 acceptance, a cold multi-version API workflow
measured 16.5 seconds: its first attachment, snapshot, and task-detail requests
consumed 4.2, 2.2, and 7.7 seconds respectively, while later requests to those
routes completed in milliseconds.

Keep the budget at the shared fixture boundary rather than adding overrides as
individual cases cross that default. The shared budget covers that bounded setup
under the existing four-worker gate, and the affected projection and lifecycle
scenarios use it rather than per-case 10- or 15-second limits. It relaxes no
behavior assertion or owner operation deadline. Other suites retain Vitest's
default, and explicit test budgets, operation deadlines, and assertions are
unchanged.

Gitea integration cost is verified in the same layer. Deterministic scenarios
pin each operation's provider requests, response bytes, and broker activations
as exact budgets, assert the operation's result alongside them, and hold local
compute only to a generous ceiling, never to a live-latency threshold.
[Gitea operation cost budgets](gitea-operation-cost-budgets.md) owns the
scenarios, the focused commands, and the explicit budget-update procedure.

## Browser Assertions And Visual Evidence

Playwright tests assert behavior and rendered-state contracts in code. Named
screenshots supplement those assertions with evidence for layout and presentation
qualities that are difficult to reduce to stable DOM checks.

Screenshots are currently manual visual-review artifacts, not golden-image
snapshots. Do not treat screenshot capture alone as a passing assertion. The
reviewer must inspect retained PNGs at original resolution for clipping, overlap,
overflow, spacing, misleading state, contradictory status, and unreadable long
content, then record defects or explicitly record that none were found. Screenshot
artifacts remain ignored by Git.

The empty-state workflow suite captures every asserted workflow state and checks
horizontal viewport overflow before capture. The exact procedure and review
checklist live in
[First Production Browser Workflow Verification](simple-workflow-verification.md).
The seeded showcase and accessible-screen inventory are documented in
[Live UI Showcase](live-ui-showcase.md). Focused browser regressions and their
named visual artifacts are documented in
[Browser Task And Session UI](browser-task-session-ui.md).

## Sustained Browser Streaming

The production workflow replay establishes an explicit earlier transcript reader
position before exercising **Jump to latest**; it does not assume that streaming
or initial history hydration has incidentally disabled follow-latest. On initial
task navigation and after owner restart it waits for the requested task-detail
response before checking its rendered cards; cold owner response latency is recorded separately from streaming
input responsiveness.

The focused browser streaming-responsiveness scenario exercises three simultaneous production
Lit views after 50,000-event mixed-history hydration, a 1,000-event burst, and at
least ten seconds of 250-events/second streaming. It records Chromium CPU profiles,
hydration/streaming long tasks, and input-to-next-paint-opportunity samples. The
100 ms p95 input target and absence of one-second stalls complement deterministic
identity, payload-work-count, cursor, and lifecycle assertions; host timing alone
is not the correctness oracle. The concrete command and limits are in
[Browser streaming responsiveness](browser-task-session-ui.md#streaming-responsiveness).

The controlled response runs the production SSE decoder and client/UI path; it
contains no model calls or private-storage browser access. A bounded real-profile
smoke independently checks actual owner/storage/transport/provider composition.
Neither layer claims a benchmark cohort or an ablation result.

## Required Repository Verification

allowed. Add `--github-excluded` to derive `github-excluded-v1`. Readiness reports
both the requested profile and its complete effective descriptor; duplicated,
unknown, or requested/effective mismatches fail startup.

Trusted launch: `node dist/mcp/main.js --directory /absolute/private/trial-dir`.
Supply the version-1 trusted session/policy/limits JSON over inherited descriptor
3 and the Brave credential over inherited descriptor 4, then close both writers.
Neither value is accepted over MCP, argv, or ordinary environment variables.
For an explicitly disposable fixture, add `--fixture` before `--directory`.
For the GitHub-excluded profile, add `--github-excluded` before `--directory`.

one JSON text block and no `structuredContent` duplicate.

isolate each trial's filesystem/mount namespace, prevent agent edits to client
configuration and binaries, and hide all other session sockets, credential and

`ResearchEngine` is a lower-level **trusted** primitive. It does not authorize
callers or reserve logical calls. The service and compatibility broker provide
those responsibilities. Do not expose its context argument or provider/cache
constructors as agent tools. Only the trusted Brave constructor receives a search
credential; the package reads no model-provider credentials or environment config.
The host owns credential provisioning, process sandboxing and filesystem access.

## Work reservations, replay and lifecycle

Work contract version 1 distinguishes `calls`, `providerAttempts`,
`fetchedDocuments`, `fetchedBytes`, `scoringPairs`, `scoringWindows`,
`scoringTokens` and `elapsedMs`. `WorkScope.run` reserves a bounded maximum before
an effect, then reconciles actual successful use. Missing counters are `null`,
not fabricated zeroes, and work requiring an unavailable dimension is refused.
Effects that fail, are cancelled, or have uncertain outcomes retain their full
reservation conservatively until a known reconciliation completes. A reservation
may commit after the caller stops waiting; cancellation never starts its effect
late or assumes that its charge was rolled back. Reconciliation is idempotent,
never exceeds the original reservation, and cannot release another effect's charge.

The reference `VolatileWorkLedger` atomically enforces the whole shared allowance
in one JS process. Logical reservations capture their own post-decision snapshot,
so out-of-order completion does not change reported admission telemetry. The
service reserves one call and its whole deadline before request validation/cache
lookup/network activity, after host authorization. Transport-envelope rejection,
changed-ID replay, pre-cancellation, offline host denial and exhausted admission
do not start work. An authorized service whose engine is offline can return an
ordinary charged offline failure; the host should deny offline work at admission.

A physical search miss reserves one provider attempt. If reservation is denied,
the provider is never invoked and evidence reports no provider attempt or
provider failure. An invoked provider that fails still reports its failed attempt.
Cache hits and coalesced waiters reserve separate logical calls but no extra provider attempts. The shared
attempt belongs to its initiating scope; its cancellation follows the shared
flight's final waiter, even if the initiating caller cancels. Namespace, provider,
query/options and exact policy separate cache keys and flights. The legacy
adapter omits the new namespace and preserves existing cache-key bytes.

A fetch reserves one document and its maximum decoded body bytes, then reconciles
the successful body's actual length. Failure retains the maximum; these are
bounded decoded-body accounting units, **not** network packet/wire-byte meters.
Redirects remain within the existing three-hop, public-address and deadline
boundary. `providerAttempts` counts search-provider invocations, not document
redirect hops. The core performs no automatic retries. Trusted future composite operations
must give each retry/fan-out effect its own reservation; tests cover that seam.

Lexical scoring reserves chunk-count times normalized focus-term-count pairs;
window/token inference counts are zero because this release does no tokenization
or neural inference. Elapsed work reserves the per-call deadline, reconciles
observed execution time before the final accounting acknowledgement. Final call
accounting and evidence acknowledgement latency is excluded from this counter; both waits
still obey the original operation deadline. Cancellation/uncertainty before
reconciliation retains the maximum until a known reconciliation completes.
Cancellation during evidence persistence does not undo already reconciled work.
This is summed execution wall time, not CPU time; concurrent calls reserve
independently. Hosts provide a consistent clock and declare exact policy limits.
No benchmark numeric policy is invented here.

`SupervisedRanker` defines explicit identity/version, result-count, positive-match
policy, source-index tie breaks, lexical fallback, work estimation and a bounded
signal-aware selection call for later prototypes. Only the pinned lexical
implementation is executed by this release. Future workers, fallback selection
and new ranking behavior require separate admission and release identities.

Replay results and document handles are transient. The service retains at most
4,096 call results, each bounded to 128 KiB, until close; ordinary host limits can
be much lower. `close()` aborts active calls and rejects later execution. Host,
caller and service cancellation are checked before replay, including completed
results; cancelled replays cannot return cached success. Each pending replay also
observes its own caller signal while waiting. Cancelling that wait returns timeout
without cancelling the original execution, altering its retained result, charging
another call or writing another evidence record. The initiating caller still owns
the execution lifetime. The engine retains at most 64 documents for ten minutes,
bound to session, capability, policy and namespace. Four initial chunks, three explicit continuation chunks,
eight continuations, 120 KiB cumulative document-visible bytes and restart loss
remain the [four-chunk release contract](four-chunk-lexical-release.md).

**The reference host is not restart-safe.** A new volatile ledger starts a new
allowance and must not be represented as recovery. Reusing the same ledger across
replacement services conserves budget and refuses already-reserved effect IDs;
it does not reconstruct old results. Durable hosts must persist reservations,
reconciliation and replay disposition atomically and fail closed on uncertain
execution. Merely labelling a custom ledger `durable` proves nothing. The
[owner research trial allowances](owner-research-trials.md) contract owns the
production implementation and restart verification of that behavior.

Authorization, ledger reservation/reconciliation and evidence hooks receive the
call's combined abort signal. The service bounds all asynchronous host waits by
the same caller/host/service cancellation and operation deadline. Hosts should
cooperate with that signal; the core cannot undo an external write or charge.
Late completions cannot resume work or change a terminal timeout into success.

The evidence sink receives only canonical compact evidence, request digest and
release identity, without queries, bodies, handles or chunks. Call accounting must
acknowledge reconciliation before the service submits success evidence. A failed
reconciliation submits failure evidence while the lifetime remains active; a
cancelled or expired reconciliation submits no new evidence. A sink failure
returns `unavailable` and its terminal failure is retained on replay without
repeating effects. Cancellation or deadline expiry returns `timeout` and starts
no new evidence write. A write already in flight may still commit; its uncertain
disposition is never overwritten or retried automatically, and replay retains
the failure. There is no automatic sink retry or success claim. Retain host
diagnostics and repair/reconcile the sink before admitting replacement execution.

### Cancellation and physical activity

Abort-raced research results remain prompt cancellation outcomes; they do not prove that their underlying effect stopped. Internally, `ResearchActivity` uses Node async context to retain promises hidden by those races. Supervised owner tools and broker requests drain this activity before publishing quiescence. Search flights have their own activity scope so every coalesced waiter retains the shared physical work. Transport tracking includes DNS completion and the HTTPS request's `close` event. This does not assert rollback of an already transmitted provider request or charge; uncertain work reservations remain charged. Standalone result and cancellation contracts are unchanged.

## Package and verification

The package supports the repository Node ranges (22.19–22.x and 24.11–24.x), uses
ES modules and exact-pins parse5 8.0.1, saxes 6.0.0 and pdfjs-dist 6.3.289 with an
independent lockfile. pdfjs-dist text extraction is pure JavaScript; its optional
`@napi-rs/canvas` native dependency installs per-platform from the same lockfile
for rendering the package never performs, so the sandboxed broker loads no native
addon on the extraction path. PDF extraction runs the pdf.js legacy build inside a
dedicated worker thread with an owned stream-expansion pre-scan, page and output
ceilings, a wall-clock watchdog, a capped worker heap, and the shared fetch
deadline; a policy admits it only through the `pdfExtraction` value.
Linux x64 on Node 22.19.0 is the verified platform here. Other platforms have no
new execution evidence; production Bubblewrap isolation remains Linux-specific.
The package has no SQLite dependency. `fixture.ts` supplies a
credential-free trusted host and fake pinned DNS/HTTPS source.

npm run build --prefix src/research/core
npm run fixture --prefix src/research/core

npx vitest run src/research --maxWorkers=4
node test/replay-three-chunk-baseline.mjs > /tmp/relayview-three-chunk-replay.json
npm run typecheck
npm run build
```

script. It contains no timestamps or credentials. `golden.json` freezes complete

structure, including IDs/order/digests and exact visible-byte accounting.
Historical three-chunk replay still checks its original complete JSON/Markdown;
its helper copies the moved supporting primitives without changing frozen
chunker code, evidence or expected results.

`npm run test:showcase`, `npm run test:workflow` and `git diff --check` as well.
Existing transport suites cover SSRF, redirect/DNS/peer validation, decompression,
size/deadline/cancellation and credential redaction through the shared modules.
The standalone tests cover host denial, strict requests, composite work ceilings,
concurrent aggregate admission/replay, cache/coalescing, cancellation, sink failure,
blocked authorization/accounting/evidence hooks and late completions, cancelled
completed and pending replay, accounting-before-evidence ordering and failure,
provider-reservation denial versus invoked-provider failure,
no cross-session/policy/namespace/capability handles and transient restart loss.

To build a portable tarball in a disposable output directory:

```zsh

(cd src/research/core && npm pack --pack-destination "$core_package_output")

# Current Orchestration Architecture

## Scope

This document describes the behavior implemented by the current TypeScript scaffold. Proposed multi-agent tracking and control behavior is documented separately in [../speculative/multi-agent-observability-and-control.md](../speculative/multi-agent-observability-and-control.md).

The bounded SQLite backup-retention contract is documented in [tracked task storage and recovery](tracked-task-storage-and-recovery.md). Startup conservatively adopts verified historical automatic snapshots, protects the exact recorded recovery point, prunes only revalidated redundant bundles, and exposes bounded path-free status plus an owner-local dry-run plan. Automatic creation and historical cleanup share the same deterministic planner and crash-safe mutation boundary.

Cross-cutting default decision rules live in [Architecture Heuristics](architecture-heuristics.md). They guide new designs but do not themselves claim that behavior is implemented.
The [task archive aggregate storage](task-archive-storage.md) persists a
role-neutral task retirement checkpoint, bounded API read projections, and
authenticated `task.archive` and `task.abandon` commands. Client controls and
navigation views remain proposed.
The [successor task lifecycle core](successor-task-lifecycle.md) persists an
internal merge-gated state machine and exact terminal release proof; its
provider/local-Git integration and public Human-review controls remain proposed.
The [external CI adapter boundary](external-ci-adapter.md) stores revisioned
project bindings and provides owner-private Gitea Actions observation for the
internal version-2 validation evidence contract.
The [remote hosting adapter boundary](remote-hosting-adapter.md) defines internal
repository/ref identity, Gitea observation, and guarded publication semantics;
revisioned owner bindings and sanitized client configuration are connected,
and owner-controlled publication verifies the exact candidate through a
durable intent.
The [pull-request adapter boundary](pull-request-adapter.md) defines separate
project admission, authenticated Gitea PR and review observation, a
policy-required draft effect, and exact-head internal merge recovery.
Agent instruction authoring follows the accepted default of
[positive action language](architecture-heuristics.md#use-positive-action-language-for-agent-instructions).
Authorization and disclosure restrictions follow
[external enforcement boundaries](architecture-heuristics.md#enforce-prohibitions-outside-the-agent),
independently of model compliance with prompt prohibitions.
Tool-call contracts follow
[minimized required model transcription](architecture-heuristics.md#minimize-required-model-transcription),
resolving owner-held canonical fields from storage instead of requiring the
model to reproduce them.

## Focused Chat And Agent Publications

New focused Chat sessions use the [durable status fallback](focused-chat-status-fallback.md): natural status publications reset a tiered owner timer, and an owner request enters only an already-running Pi model boundary. Timers cannot wake agents or create Human review influence.

Focused Chat provides a retained-history focused-conversation projection and
route-addressable Implementer Chat. New task-bound Planner, Implementer, and
Reviewer Chat use an owner-mediated, non-interrupting inbox and the private
`publish_focused_chat_message` tool rather than transcript inference. Exact
user messages and explicit agent publications are durable events in the existing
owner ledger; private prompts, reasoning, tools, protocol traffic, reports, and
telemetry remain in Dashboard. New roles use focused transport v6 with [natural acknowledgements](natural-agent-acknowledgements.md). Implementers and Plan reviewers retain v5 delivery:
active inboxes reach Pi after the current tool batch through native streaming
steer, preserving the active tool and agent loop. Admission requires the matching
Pi user-message event, rather than the RPC queue acknowledgement. Pre-v5
Implementer/Reviewer transports and current Planner transports keep the owner's
settlement-aware turn queue. Idle delivery starts a normal prompt. See the
[Implementer delivery contract](implementer-communication-context.md) and
[Reviewer conversation/judgment contract](reviewer-communication-context.md).
A timed-out or restart-interrupted admission is failed closed as
delivery-ambiguous and is never automatically redelivered. Retained sessions
without the focused-transport assignment marker remain readable through the
compatibility projection. Both communication-context ablation arms
receive identical tool, prompt, inbox, publication, and replay semantics.
Eligible task-bound roles must emit a brief, human-friendly, uncorrelated
`progress` publication when they complete one meaningful internal work phase and
begin the next, so later Human inspection reveals both the completed result and

# Testing Strategy

## Purpose

RelayView uses a layered testing strategy shaped like a testing pyramid. Most
behavior should be verified by deterministic unit and bounded-integration tests.
Progressively smaller suites exercise the built browser, the assembled production
workflow, and finally real model-provider behavior.

This document defines the responsibility of each layer and the defaults for
placing new coverage. It intentionally does not prescribe fixed test counts or
ratios. The important invariant is that most behavioral coverage remains below
the browser and real-provider layers, while a small number of higher-level tests
prove that the boundaries compose correctly.

Tests are specification artifacts. A behavioral change is incomplete until the
appropriate layer verifies its success path, important failures, recovery or
state transitions, and externally visible contract.

## Layers

| Layer | Primary commands | Responsibility | Default characteristics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit and bounded integration | `npm test` | Domain logic, state machines, storage, API and protocol contracts, security boundaries, adapters, and focused process interactions | Numerous, deterministic, isolated, and as fast as the boundary permits |
| Browser integration | `npm run test:browser` | Built Lit UI behavior, routing, component contracts, owner-client integration, accessibility-relevant controls, responsive layout, and large-data behavior | Fewer scenarios using controlled fixtures; assertions focus on behavior and rendered state |
| Seeded production showcase | `npm run test:showcase` | Production browser, owner API, durable store, event path, supervisor, and Git-status presentation with representative pre-populated state | Small deterministic suite for assembled evidence surfaces and stable visual review |
| Empty-state production workflow | `npm run test:workflow` | Public New Task submission through planner finalization, automatic implementation handoff, validation, Git isolation, session control, restart/recovery, and typed failure behavior | Very small deterministic end-to-end suite using Pi-compatible fake processes and real local infrastructure boundaries |
| Real-profile smoke | Manifest-backed workflow smoke and documented admission checks | Actual Pi and model-provider usability, credential delivery, model assignment, tool loops, and a real repository edit | Narrow, explicit, potentially costly, and run only when the affected provider or production boundary requires it |

The first layer is not required to consist only of pure in-memory unit tests.
SQLite, filesystem, subprocess, and assembled-service tests belong there when
those dependencies are the smallest useful boundary for the behavior. Keep each
test focused and deterministic, and avoid promoting coverage to Playwright merely
because the implementation crosses modules.

## Choosing A Layer

Place a regression at the lowest layer that can faithfully prove the behavior:

1. Prefer a focused Vitest test for logic, persistence, protocol, state, failure,
   recovery, and security invariants.
2. Add browser integration coverage when correctness depends on rendering,
   browser events, focus, responsive layout, accessibility semantics, routing,
   or the browser-facing client contract.
3. Extend a production-path workflow scenario only when the risk is in the
   composition of owner, store, events, process supervision, Git, private tools,
   and browser behavior. Prefer extending an existing scenario over adding a new
   full lifecycle when that preserves fault isolation and readability.
4. Require a real-profile smoke only when deterministic substitutes cannot prove
   provider compatibility, credentials, model assignment, or actual model/tool
   behavior.

Higher-level coverage complements rather than replaces lower-level coverage. A
workflow regression should normally have focused tests for its important domain
and failure rules, while the workflow test proves that those rules remain wired
together through production boundaries.

## Determinism And Isolation

The default automated suites must not depend on public network access, provider
availability, production credentials, or nondeterministic model output. Use
controlled clocks, fixtures, disposable repositories and databases, and
Pi-compatible fake processes as appropriate. Tests must not read or retain
credentials, private provider diagnostics, or unrelated host state.

Process-backed tests remain part of the normal Vitest layer but must have bounded
startup, shutdown, output, and failure behavior. The standard `npm test` command
caps Vitest at four workers because greater file concurrency reproducibly caused
unrelated process-backed failures; see
[Source Layout And Retrieval Evidence](../historical/issue-259-source-layout-evidence.md).

Test files importing `src/api/api-test-fixtures.ts` use a 30-second default
through Vitest's file-local runtime configuration. These bounded integration
suites include Git, SQLite, HTTP schema setup, workflow execution, and shutdown.
<!-- keep-issue-ref: verification-run — the 30-second budget's only support is these two identified measurement runs -->
Two measurements support that budget. During #402 acceptance, seven cases across
benchmark, workflow, HTTP client, and task-memory suites exceeded the generic
five-second default; all completed their assertions in roughly 4.7–6.3 seconds in
isolated diagnostics. During #516 acceptance, a cold multi-version API workflow
measured 16.5 seconds: its first attachment, snapshot, and task-detail requests
consumed 4.2, 2.2, and 7.7 seconds respectively, while later requests to those
routes completed in milliseconds.

Keep the budget at the shared fixture boundary rather than adding overrides as
individual cases cross that default. The shared budget covers that bounded setup
under the existing four-worker gate, and the affected projection and lifecycle
scenarios use it rather than per-case 10- or 15-second limits. It relaxes no
behavior assertion or owner operation deadline. Other suites retain Vitest's
default, and explicit test budgets, operation deadlines, and assertions are
unchanged.

Gitea integration cost is verified in the same layer. Deterministic scenarios
pin each operation's provider requests, response bytes, and broker activations
as exact budgets, assert the operation's result alongside them, and hold local
compute only to a generous ceiling, never to a live-latency threshold.
[Gitea operation cost budgets](gitea-operation-cost-budgets.md) owns the
scenarios, the focused commands, and the explicit budget-update procedure.

## Browser Assertions And Visual Evidence

Playwright tests assert behavior and rendered-state contracts in code. Named
screenshots supplement those assertions with evidence for layout and presentation
qualities that are difficult to reduce to stable DOM checks.

Screenshots are currently manual visual-review artifacts, not golden-image
snapshots. Do not treat screenshot capture alone as a passing assertion. The
reviewer must inspect retained PNGs at original resolution for clipping, overlap,
overflow, spacing, misleading state, contradictory status, and unreadable long
content, then record defects or explicitly record that none were found. Screenshot
artifacts remain ignored by Git.

The empty-state workflow suite captures every asserted workflow state and checks
horizontal viewport overflow before capture. The exact procedure and review
checklist live in
[First Production Browser Workflow Verification](simple-workflow-verification.md).
The seeded showcase and accessible-screen inventory are documented in
[Live UI Showcase](live-ui-showcase.md). Focused browser regressions and their
named visual artifacts are documented in
[Browser Task And Session UI](browser-task-session-ui.md).

## Sustained Browser Streaming

The production workflow replay establishes an explicit earlier transcript reader
position before exercising **Jump to latest**; it does not assume that streaming
or initial history hydration has incidentally disabled follow-latest. On initial
task navigation and after owner restart it waits for the requested task-detail
response before checking its rendered cards; cold owner response latency is recorded separately from streaming
input responsiveness.

The focused browser streaming-responsiveness scenario exercises three simultaneous production
Lit views after 50,000-event mixed-history hydration, a 1,000-event burst, and at
least ten seconds of 250-events/second streaming. It records Chromium CPU profiles,
hydration/streaming long tasks, and input-to-next-paint-opportunity samples. The
100 ms p95 input target and absence of one-second stalls complement deterministic
identity, payload-work-count, cursor, and lifecycle assertions; host timing alone
is not the correctness oracle. The concrete command and limits are in
[Browser streaming responsiveness](browser-task-session-ui.md#streaming-responsiveness).

The controlled response runs the production SSE decoder and client/UI path; it
contains no model calls or private-storage browser access. A bounded real-profile
smoke independently checks actual owner/storage/transport/provider composition.
Neither layer claims a benchmark cohort or an ablation result.

# RelayView research MCP 1.1.0

Thin MCP stdio bridge and supervised Unix-socket service over the shared
`@relayview/research-core` 1.1.0 source, selection `lexical-v2-initial-4`.
The tarball includes that exact compiled source, parse5 8.0.1 and saxes 6.0.0
through its shrinkwrap. It does not contain a second ranker or import the owner.

Use Node 22.19–22.x or 24.11–24.x on Linux. Build with `npm run build`, inspect
`npm run artifact`, and pack with `npm pack`. Run the credential-free transport
check with `node dist/mcp/smoke.js` (requires Bubblewrap). The fixture calls a
supervised service through a network-disabled stdio bridge.

With no source option, the launcher derives `public-web-v1` and GitHub remains
allowed. Add `--github-excluded` to derive `github-excluded-v1`. Readiness reports
both the requested profile and its complete effective descriptor; duplicated,
unknown, or requested/effective mismatches fail startup.

Trusted launch: `node dist/mcp/main.js --directory /absolute/private/trial-dir`.
Supply the version-1 trusted session/policy/limits JSON over inherited descriptor
3 and the Brave credential over inherited descriptor 4, then close both writers.
Neither value is accepted over MCP, argv, or ordinary environment variables.
For an explicitly disposable fixture, add `--fixture` before `--directory`.
For the GitHub-excluded profile, add `--github-excluded` before `--directory`.

Client command: `node dist/mcp/bridge.js /absolute/private/trial-dir/research.sock`.
Only `web_search` and `web_fetch` are exposed. Core requests, canonical results,
accounting and private-address rules retain their shared meaning. Responses have
one JSON text block and no `structuredContent` duplicate.

The private socket mount is the session capability. The trusted supervisor must
isolate each trial's filesystem/mount namespace, prevent agent edits to client
configuration and binaries, and hide all other session sockets, credential and
control paths. A same-UID unrestricted shell is outside that boundary. Do not
present socket file modes as protection from the same unrestricted user.

This standalone host uses volatile accounting and keeps a `started` marker.
Bridge reconnect preserves the live service allowance. Service restart in the
same directory is refused; do not delete the marker to resume a trial. Durable
benchmark provisioning/accounting is separate integration work. Stop the whole
trial on sidecar loss; only a newly authorized trial may receive fresh state.

The repository's `docs/authoritative/research-mcp.md` contains complete setup,
pinned native verification, live smoke, recovery, cleanup and evidence limits.

`ResearchEngine` is a lower-level **trusted** primitive. It does not authorize
callers or reserve logical calls. The service and compatibility broker provide
those responsibilities. Do not expose its context argument or provider/cache
constructors as agent tools. Only the trusted Brave constructor receives a search
credential; the package reads no model-provider credentials or environment config.
The host owns credential provisioning, process sandboxing and filesystem access.

## Work reservations, replay and lifecycle

Work contract version 1 distinguishes `calls`, `providerAttempts`,
`fetchedDocuments`, `fetchedBytes`, `scoringPairs`, `scoringWindows`,
`scoringTokens` and `elapsedMs`. `WorkScope.run` reserves a bounded maximum before
an effect, then reconciles actual successful use. Missing counters are `null`,
not fabricated zeroes, and work requiring an unavailable dimension is refused.
Effects that fail, are cancelled, or have uncertain outcomes retain their full
reservation conservatively until a known reconciliation completes. A reservation
may commit after the caller stops waiting; cancellation never starts its effect
late or assumes that its charge was rolled back. Reconciliation is idempotent,
never exceeds the original reservation, and cannot release another effect's charge.

The reference `VolatileWorkLedger` atomically enforces the whole shared allowance
in one JS process. Logical reservations capture their own post-decision snapshot,
so out-of-order completion does not change reported admission telemetry. The
service reserves one call and its whole deadline before request validation/cache
lookup/network activity, after host authorization. Transport-envelope rejection,
changed-ID replay, pre-cancellation, offline host denial and exhausted admission
do not start work. An authorized service whose engine is offline can return an
ordinary charged offline failure; the host should deny offline work at admission.

A physical search miss reserves one provider attempt. If reservation is denied,
the provider is never invoked and evidence reports no provider attempt or
provider failure. An invoked provider that fails still reports its failed attempt.
Cache hits and coalesced waiters reserve separate logical calls but no extra provider attempts. The shared
attempt belongs to its initiating scope; its cancellation follows the shared
flight's final waiter, even if the initiating caller cancels. Namespace, provider,
query/options and exact policy separate cache keys and flights. The legacy
adapter omits the new namespace and preserves existing cache-key bytes.

A fetch reserves one document and its maximum decoded body bytes, then reconciles
the successful body's actual length. Failure retains the maximum; these are
bounded decoded-body accounting units, **not** network packet/wire-byte meters.
Redirects remain within the existing three-hop, public-address and deadline
boundary. `providerAttempts` counts search-provider invocations, not document
redirect hops. The core performs no automatic retries. Trusted future composite operations
must give each retry/fan-out effect its own reservation; tests cover that seam.

Lexical scoring reserves chunk-count times normalized focus-term-count pairs;
window/token inference counts are zero because this release does no tokenization
or neural inference. Elapsed work reserves the per-call deadline, reconciles
observed execution time before the final accounting acknowledgement. Final call
accounting and evidence acknowledgement latency is excluded from this counter; both waits
still obey the original operation deadline. Cancellation/uncertainty before
reconciliation retains the maximum until a known reconciliation completes.
Cancellation during evidence persistence does not undo already reconciled work.
This is summed execution wall time, not CPU time; concurrent calls reserve
independently. Hosts provide a consistent clock and declare exact policy limits.
No benchmark numeric policy is invented here.

`SupervisedRanker` defines explicit identity/version, result-count, positive-match
policy, source-index tie breaks, lexical fallback, work estimation and a bounded
signal-aware selection call for later prototypes. Only the pinned lexical
implementation is executed by this release. Future workers, fallback selection
and new ranking behavior require separate admission and release identities.

Replay results and document handles are transient. The service retains at most
4,096 call results, each bounded to 128 KiB, until close; ordinary host limits can
be much lower. `close()` aborts active calls and rejects later execution. Host,
caller and service cancellation are checked before replay, including completed
results; cancelled replays cannot return cached success. Each pending replay also
observes its own caller signal while waiting. Cancelling that wait returns timeout
without cancelling the original execution, altering its retained result, charging
another call or writing another evidence record. The initiating caller still owns
the execution lifetime. The engine retains at most 64 documents for ten minutes,
bound to session, capability, policy and namespace. Four initial chunks, three explicit continuation chunks,
eight continuations, 120 KiB cumulative document-visible bytes and restart loss
remain the [four-chunk release contract](four-chunk-lexical-release.md).

**The reference host is not restart-safe.** A new volatile ledger starts a new
allowance and must not be represented as recovery. Reusing the same ledger across
replacement services conserves budget and refuses already-reserved effect IDs;
it does not reconstruct old results. Durable hosts must persist reservations,
reconciliation and replay disposition atomically and fail closed on uncertain
execution. Merely labelling a custom ledger `durable` proves nothing. The
[owner research trial allowances](owner-research-trials.md) contract owns the
production implementation and restart verification of that behavior.

Authorization, ledger reservation/reconciliation and evidence hooks receive the
call's combined abort signal. The service bounds all asynchronous host waits by
the same caller/host/service cancellation and operation deadline. Hosts should
cooperate with that signal; the core cannot undo an external write or charge.
Late completions cannot resume work or change a terminal timeout into success.

The evidence sink receives only canonical compact evidence, request digest and
release identity, without queries, bodies, handles or chunks. Call accounting must
acknowledge reconciliation before the service submits success evidence. A failed
reconciliation submits failure evidence while the lifetime remains active; a
cancelled or expired reconciliation submits no new evidence. A sink failure
returns `unavailable` and its terminal failure is retained on replay without
repeating effects. Cancellation or deadline expiry returns `timeout` and starts
no new evidence write. A write already in flight may still commit; its uncertain
disposition is never overwritten or retried automatically, and replay retains
the failure. There is no automatic sink retry or success claim. Retain host
diagnostics and repair/reconcile the sink before admitting replacement execution.

### Cancellation and physical activity

Abort-raced research results remain prompt cancellation outcomes; they do not prove that their underlying effect stopped. Internally, `ResearchActivity` uses Node async context to retain promises hidden by those races. Supervised owner tools and broker requests drain this activity before publishing quiescence. Search flights have their own activity scope so every coalesced waiter retains the shared physical work. Transport tracking includes DNS completion and the HTTPS request's `close` event. This does not assert rollback of an already transmitted provider request or charge; uncertain work reservations remain charged. Standalone result and cancellation contracts are unchanged.

## Package and verification

The package supports the repository Node ranges (22.19–22.x and 24.11–24.x), uses
ES modules and exact-pins parse5 8.0.1, saxes 6.0.0 and pdfjs-dist 6.3.289 with an
independent lockfile. pdfjs-dist text extraction is pure JavaScript; its optional
`@napi-rs/canvas` native dependency installs per-platform from the same lockfile
for rendering the package never performs, so the sandboxed broker loads no native
addon on the extraction path. PDF extraction runs the pdf.js legacy build inside a
dedicated worker thread with an owned stream-expansion pre-scan, page and output
ceilings, a wall-clock watchdog, a capped worker heap, and the shared fetch
deadline; a policy admits it only through the `pdfExtraction` value.
Linux x64 on Node 22.19.0 is the verified platform here. Other platforms have no
new execution evidence; production Bubblewrap isolation remains Linux-specific.
The package has no SQLite dependency. `fixture.ts` supplies a
credential-free trusted host and fake pinned DNS/HTTPS source.

# Testing Strategy

## Purpose

RelayView uses a layered testing strategy shaped like a testing pyramid. Most
behavior should be verified by deterministic unit and bounded-integration tests.
Progressively smaller suites exercise the built browser, the assembled production
workflow, and finally real model-provider behavior.

This document defines the responsibility of each layer and the defaults for
placing new coverage. It intentionally does not prescribe fixed test counts or
ratios. The important invariant is that most behavioral coverage remains below
the browser and real-provider layers, while a small number of higher-level tests
prove that the boundaries compose correctly.

Tests are specification artifacts. A behavioral change is incomplete until the
appropriate layer verifies its success path, important failures, recovery or
state transitions, and externally visible contract.

## Layers

| Layer | Primary commands | Responsibility | Default characteristics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit and bounded integration | `npm test` | Domain logic, state machines, storage, API and protocol contracts, security boundaries, adapters, and focused process interactions | Numerous, deterministic, isolated, and as fast as the boundary permits |
| Browser integration | `npm run test:browser` | Built Lit UI behavior, routing, component contracts, owner-client integration, accessibility-relevant controls, responsive layout, and large-data behavior | Fewer scenarios using controlled fixtures; assertions focus on behavior and rendered state |
| Seeded production showcase | `npm run test:showcase` | Production browser, owner API, durable store, event path, supervisor, and Git-status presentation with representative pre-populated state | Small deterministic suite for assembled evidence surfaces and stable visual review |
| Empty-state production workflow | `npm run test:workflow` | Public New Task submission through planner finalization, automatic implementation handoff, validation, Git isolation, session control, restart/recovery, and typed failure behavior | Very small deterministic end-to-end suite using Pi-compatible fake processes and real local infrastructure boundaries |
| Real-profile smoke | Manifest-backed workflow smoke and documented admission checks | Actual Pi and model-provider usability, credential delivery, model assignment, tool loops, and a real repository edit | Narrow, explicit, potentially costly, and run only when the affected provider or production boundary requires it |

The first layer is not required to consist only of pure in-memory unit tests.
SQLite, filesystem, subprocess, and assembled-service tests belong there when
those dependencies are the smallest useful boundary for the behavior. Keep each
test focused and deterministic, and avoid promoting coverage to Playwright merely
because the implementation crosses modules.

## Choosing A Layer

Place a regression at the lowest layer that can faithfully prove the behavior:

1. Prefer a focused Vitest test for logic, persistence, protocol, state, failure,
   recovery, and security invariants.
2. Add browser integration coverage when correctness depends on rendering,
   browser events, focus, responsive layout, accessibility semantics, routing,
   or the browser-facing client contract.
3. Extend a production-path workflow scenario only when the risk is in the
   composition of owner, store, events, process supervision, Git, private tools,
   and browser behavior. Prefer extending an existing scenario over adding a new
   full lifecycle when that preserves fault isolation and readability.
4. Require a real-profile smoke only when deterministic substitutes cannot prove
   provider compatibility, credentials, model assignment, or actual model/tool
   behavior.

Higher-level coverage complements rather than replaces lower-level coverage. A
workflow regression should normally have focused tests for its important domain
and failure rules, while the workflow test proves that those rules remain wired
together through production boundaries.

## Determinism And Isolation

The default automated suites must not depend on public network access, provider
availability, production credentials, or nondeterministic model output. Use
controlled clocks, fixtures, disposable repositories and databases, and
Pi-compatible fake processes as appropriate. Tests must not read or retain
credentials, private provider diagnostics, or unrelated host state.

Process-backed tests remain part of the normal Vitest layer but must have bounded
startup, shutdown, output, and failure behavior. The standard `npm test` command
caps Vitest at four workers because greater file concurrency reproducibly caused
unrelated process-backed failures; see
[Source Layout And Retrieval Evidence](../historical/issue-259-source-layout-evidence.md).

Test files importing `src/api/api-test-fixtures.ts` use a 30-second default
through Vitest's file-local runtime configuration. These bounded integration
suites include Git, SQLite, HTTP schema setup, workflow execution, and shutdown.
<!-- keep-issue-ref: verification-run — the 30-second budget's only support is these two identified measurement runs -->
Two measurements support that budget. During #402 acceptance, seven cases across
benchmark, workflow, HTTP client, and task-memory suites exceeded the generic
five-second default; all completed their assertions in roughly 4.7–6.3 seconds in
isolated diagnostics. During #516 acceptance, a cold multi-version API workflow
measured 16.5 seconds: its first attachment, snapshot, and task-detail requests
consumed 4.2, 2.2, and 7.7 seconds respectively, while later requests to those
routes completed in milliseconds.

Keep the budget at the shared fixture boundary rather than adding overrides as
individual cases cross that default. The shared budget covers that bounded setup
under the existing four-worker gate, and the affected projection and lifecycle
scenarios use it rather than per-case 10- or 15-second limits. It relaxes no
behavior assertion or owner operation deadline. Other suites retain Vitest's
default, and explicit test budgets, operation deadlines, and assertions are
unchanged.

Gitea integration cost is verified in the same layer. Deterministic scenarios
pin each operation's provider requests, response bytes, and broker activations
as exact budgets, assert the operation's result alongside them, and hold local
compute only to a generous ceiling, never to a live-latency threshold.
[Gitea operation cost budgets](gitea-operation-cost-budgets.md) owns the
scenarios, the focused commands, and the explicit budget-update procedure.

## Browser Assertions And Visual Evidence

Playwright tests assert behavior and rendered-state contracts in code. Named
screenshots supplement those assertions with evidence for layout and presentation
qualities that are difficult to reduce to stable DOM checks.

Screenshots are currently manual visual-review artifacts, not golden-image
snapshots. Do not treat screenshot capture alone as a passing assertion. The
reviewer must inspect retained PNGs at original resolution for clipping, overlap,
overflow, spacing, misleading state, contradictory status, and unreadable long
content, then record defects or explicitly record that none were found. Screenshot
artifacts remain ignored by Git.

The empty-state workflow suite captures every asserted workflow state and checks
horizontal viewport overflow before capture. The exact procedure and review
checklist live in
[First Production Browser Workflow Verification](simple-workflow-verification.md).
The seeded showcase and accessible-screen inventory are documented in
[Live UI Showcase](live-ui-showcase.md). Focused browser regressions and their
named visual artifacts are documented in
[Browser Task And Session UI](browser-task-session-ui.md).

## Sustained Browser Streaming

The production workflow replay establishes an explicit earlier transcript reader
position before exercising **Jump to latest**; it does not assume that streaming
or initial history hydration has incidentally disabled follow-latest. On initial
task navigation and after owner restart it waits for the requested task-detail
response before checking its rendered cards; cold owner response latency is recorded separately from streaming
input responsiveness.

The focused browser streaming-responsiveness scenario exercises three simultaneous production
Lit views after 50,000-event mixed-history hydration, a 1,000-event burst, and at
least ten seconds of 250-events/second streaming. It records Chromium CPU profiles,
hydration/streaming long tasks, and input-to-next-paint-opportunity samples. The
100 ms p95 input target and absence of one-second stalls complement deterministic
identity, payload-work-count, cursor, and lifecycle assertions; host timing alone
is not the correctness oracle. The concrete command and limits are in
[Browser streaming responsiveness](browser-task-session-ui.md#streaming-responsiveness).

The controlled response runs the production SSE decoder and client/UI path; it
contains no model calls or private-storage browser access. A bounded real-profile
smoke independently checks actual owner/storage/transport/provider composition.
Neither layer claims a benchmark cohort or an ablation result.

# Research MCP sidecar loss: recovery decision and implementation plan

**Status: proposed supervisor integration; not implemented here.** Current standalone behavior is in [Bounded shared research MCP](../authoritative/research-mcp.md). The owner-managed SQLite research trial described in [Owner research trial allowances](../authoritative/owner-research-trials.md) is a different host; it does not make the standalone MCP sidecar's volatile ledger durable. External benchmark namespace provisioning and total trial scheduling belong to `agent-harness-evals`. This plan does not authorize a benchmark or change an admitted cohort.

## Decision

**Fail closed on supervised sidecar disappearance during a standalone trial.** Mark the trial interrupted/terminal, stop the native client and its bridge(s), revoke their socket mount, and preserve the trial's `started` marker and compact diagnostics. Do not restart `main.js` in that trial, delete the marker, switch it to another socket, or transparently retry a tool call. A new trial requires fresh external authorization, identity, private directory, socket mount and allowance; it must not masquerade as continuation of the interrupted trial. A bridge reconnect is permissible only while the *same* supervised service is alive with its existing ledger. Service loss is not equivalent to a bridge disconnect. A missing readiness response or an ambiguous supervisor health result also fails closed; readiness proves transport setup, not a live provider.

This preserves the product's least-privilege and traceable-handoff direction at the cost of availability and potentially wasted work. It avoids pretending an unknown provider effect was free. No experimental quality mechanism is added: **ablation decision: not_required** for the safety boundary; never make credential confinement, work accounting or evidence integrity optional. If the evaluation owner wants to compare availability strategies, that is a separate, explicitly admitted experiment, not a flag that bypasses these invariants.

## Why the present bridge cannot safely restart the service

- `bridge.ts` checks that an absolute path is a same-UID, mode-0600 socket, then pipes MCP stdio bytes to it; it does not authenticate trial/session/epoch or pin the socket inode after path lookup. `sidecar.ts` checks the owner and mode of an existing private directory, creates and fsyncs `started` with exclusive creation **before** listen, then binds `research.sock`. Normal close removes only the socket; a crash may leave it. Socket path reuse, a replacement bind mount, or deletion of `started` could let a surviving or newly launched bridge reach a different service. Same UID plus file modes is not isolation from an unrestricted same-UID agent. The harness must hide other sockets, writable service paths, credentials and client configuration and must not recycle the mounted address into a different trial.
- `main.ts` reads bounded setup JSON on fd 3 and Brave credential on fd 4, closes both after bootstrap and reports only release, source-policy descriptor, policy and setup digest on private stdout; compact evidence goes to supervisor stderr. The bridge must never be given either descriptor, setup in argv/env/workspace, or an unrestricted host view. A relaunch would require *trusted* reprovisioning, not an agent request. Diagnostic capture must remain bounded and redacted.
- `main.ts` constructs `VolatileWorkLedger`; `ResearchService` retains results and the engine retains document handles only in memory. An MCP connection creates private core call IDs; JSON-RPC IDs are unique only within that connection and reconnects are **new calls**, not durable replay IDs. Work reserves calls and maximum effect work before execution; failed, cancelled and uncertain effects remain charged. A new process has no reliable knowledge of prior reservations, completion, in-flight provider effects, evidence acknowledgements or handle state. Recreating limits from fd 3 resets quota. The marker is an intentional one-start fence, not a recoverable ledger. The production owner's SQLite `WorkLedger` and restart/export semantics cannot be inferred for this standalone package.

## Staged delivery

1. **Supervisor fail-closed boundary (recommended scope).** At trial admission, record the frozen trial/session/capability/cache namespace, policy/source profile, setup digest, MCP/core artifact and limits, credential binding identifier (not secret bytes), directory/mount identity, supervised PID/process identity and client assignment outside the agent workspace. Enforce the original deadline and frozen artifact/policy and do not automatically retry provider operations. A durable ledger alone is insufficient if another unfenced process can still serve.
4. **If stage 3 is authorized, change transport admission too.** The supervisor must stop/fence and prove old service and bridges quiescent before activating a replacement; create a new generation-specific socket in a fresh private path and remount only for a deliberately relaunched, assigned client. Bind a supervisor-supplied expected trial/session/generation to an authenticated private bridge-to-sidecar handshake **before** MCP initialization/tool execution; reject missing, mismatched, stale or replayed generation. The handshake credential must not be a model-visible MCP argument, public env value or shared workspace file. Socket owner/mode and path are necessary but not sufficient. Never reuse an old mounted socket path for a different session, including after rollback. Pin readiness to frozen setup/artifact and verify the durable ledger's generation before announcing availability. Verify with kill/restart/rebind race tests across separate trials and a deliberately stale client, including mid-reservation and late write; the old client must fail rather than connect to the new session. Do not enable restart if any of these proofs fail.

## Verification, release and rollback gates

For stage 1, focused local checks are `npx vitest run src/research/mcp/process.test.ts src/research/mcp/protocol.test.ts src/research/core --maxWorkers=4`, `npm run verify:research-mcp`, `npm run typecheck`, and `git diff --check`, plus new supervisor fixture tests in the external harness when wired. Pin results to the candidate commit/package digest. The existing deterministic package smoke proves network denial in the bridge, not namespace containment or crash supervision; the owner trial SQLite tests prove a *different* durable integration. A native-client smoke validates only transport/serialization, not a real credential route. Record exact test output and an operator-approved live check separately. Promote only verified behavior to the authoritative MCP/recovery documentation.

Rollback of stage 1 restores the previous admitted whole MCP/core artifact and external supervisor configuration **for a newly authorized trial** after stopping old clients, preserving evidence and terminal marker; never roll a database or directory back and resume the interrupted identity. If a later durable restart feature violates accounting, confinement or stale-client fencing, disable restart, fail closed on sidecar loss, retain ledger/evidence for audit, and require a fresh authorized trial under a frozen artifact. If an admitted benchmark cohort has started, a rollback is not a silent in-place cohort change; obtain a new admission decision.

sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- grep: Search file contents for patterns (respects .gitignore)
- find: Find files by glob pattern (respects .gitignore)
- ls: List directory contents

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: grep
toolsAdded.description: Search file contents for a pattern. Returns matching lines with file paths and line numbers. Respects .gitignore. Output is truncated to 100 matches or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Long lines are truncated to 500 chars.

path.description: Directory or file to search (default: current directory)

glob.description: Filter files by glob pattern, e.g. '*.ts' or '**/*.spec.ts'

literal.description: Treat pattern as literal string instead of regex (default: false)

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (default: 0)

limit.description: Maximum number of matches to return (default: 100)

toolsAdded.name: find
toolsAdded.description: Search for files by glob pattern. Returns matching file paths relative to the search directory. Respects .gitignore. Output is truncated to 1000 results or 50KB (whichever is hit first).

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match files, e.g. '*.ts', '**/*.json', or 'src/**/*.spec.ts'

path.description: Directory to search in (default: current directory)

toolsAdded.name: ls
toolsAdded.description: List directory contents. Returns entries sorted alphabetically, with '/' suffix for directories. Includes dotfiles. Output is truncated to 500 entries or 50KB (whichever is hit first).

limit.description: Maximum number of entries to return (default: 500)

toolsAdded.name: web_search
toolsAdded.description: Search the web using the current supported provider (Google Gemini, xAI Grok, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Ollama, or OpenCode Zen/Go). Optionally include URLs to analyze alongside search results.

query.description: The search query or question to answer

urls.description: Additional URLs to analyze along with search (up to 20)

toolsAdded.name: web_fetch
toolsAdded.description:
Retrieves and extracts the main content of a web page as markdown.

Include a 'prompt' parameter to have an LLM distill the page down to just the information you need — this saves significant context compared to ingesting raw page content.
Without a prompt, the full extracted markdown is returned (or a structured overview if the page is large).

Batch mode: use 'pages' instead of 'url' to fetch multiple URLs in a single call. Each entry can have its own prompt.
This is much faster than making separate web_fetch calls when you need content from several pages.
The 'url' and 'pages' parameters are mutually exclusive. Maximum 10 pages per batch.

When to use something else:
- The gh CLI (via bash) for anything on GitHub — issues, PRs, repo contents, API calls.

Behavior notes:
- URLs must include the scheme (e.g. https://). Plain HTTP is silently upgraded to HTTPS.
- Fetched content is held in a short-lived cache, so asking multiple questions about the same page is cheap.
- Cross-host redirects are surfaced rather than followed — make a second request to the target URL.
- No files or external state are modified by this tool.

url.description: Fully-formed URL to fetch (e.g., https://example.com/page). Mutually exclusive with 'pages'.

prompt.description: What information to extract from the page. Strongly recommended — the page content will be processed by a fast LLM and only relevant information returned. Omit only if you need the full raw content. Only used with 'url', not 'pages'.
What information to extract from this page

pages.description: Array of pages to fetch concurrently (max 10). Mutually exclusive with 'url'. Each entry can have its own prompt.
